stem: In the context of web applications, what is a **server**?

options.text: A program that runs once, prints its result and terminates
Any computer that has a web browser installed
The internet service provider that connects your computer to the internet
A program (and, by extension, the machine running it) that keeps running and can be reached through the network to answer requests

explanation: A server is a long-running program that never stops and can be accessed through the network: it waits for requests (e.g. HTTP requests) and sends back responses. The word designates both the program and the computer running it.

distractor_notes.a: A server is precisely a program that does not stop after one run.
distractor_notes.b: Having a browser makes a computer a client, not a server.
distractor_notes.c: The ISP gives you access to the internet; it is not the program answering your request.

verify.reference: Slide 284 'Servers': a program that never stops and can be accessed through the network

stem: How is a home computer usually connected to the internet?

options.text: Directly, like the servers of big websites
Through an Internet Service Provider (ISP), which is itself connected to the internet
Through the DNS server of each website it visits
Through the web browser, which acts as an ISP

explanation: Only some machines (servers, ISPs) are directly connected to the internet; your computer is connected to an ISP, which is in turn connected to the internet and relays your traffic.

distractor_notes.a: The course stresses that your computer is NOT directly connected to the internet.
distractor_notes.c: DNS translates names into IP addresses; it does not provide connectivity.
distractor_notes.d: The browser is a client program; it does not provide network access.

verify.reference: Slide 287 'The internet: a big computer network' - your computer is connected to an ISP

stem: What is **DNS resolution**?

options.text: Translating a domain name such as `github.com` into the IP address of the server
Splitting an HTTP response into packets
Choosing the port number of the server from the scheme of the URL
Turning the HTML of a page into a rendered web page

explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) resolution maps a human-readable domain name to an IP address. The ISP keeps a table domain name -> IP address and, when it does not know a name, asks other nodes of the network recursively.

distractor_notes.b: Packets are how large responses travel on the network, unrelated to names.
distractor_notes.c: The default port comes from the scheme (80 for http, 443 for https), not from DNS.
distractor_notes.d: Rendering is done by the browser.

stem: Which of the following are valid IPv4 addresses? Select all that apply.
explanation: An IPv4 address is made of 4 numbers separated by dots, each between 0 and 255 (one byte). 89.259.29.11 and 256.1.1.1 contain a number above 255, so they are invalid. 127.0.0.1 is valid: it is the loopback address of your own machine.

distractor_notes.c: 256 does not fit in one byte (the maximum is 255).
distractor_notes.d: 259 > 255: each of the 4 numbers is a single byte (0-255). This address appears in a course diagram only as an illustration.

stem: Why does a client need to specify a **port** when it connects to a server machine?

options.text: Because the port identifies the ISP of the client
Because one machine can run several server programs, and each one listens on its own port
Because the port is the encrypted version of the IP address
Because the port tells the browser how to render the page

explanation: A single computer (one IP address) may run an HTTP server, an API server, a mail server, a database... The port number selects which of these programs receives the request (e.g. 443 for an HTTPS server).

distractor_notes.a: The ISP is not identified by a port.
distractor_notes.c: The IP address identifies the machine and the port identifies the program on that machine; nothing is encrypted.
distractor_notes.d: Rendering depends on the HTML received, not on the port.

verify.reference: Slide 292 'What is a port?' - every server listens to a specific port; slide 316

stem: Which of the following is correct about a large HTTP response (for instance a big image)?

options.text: It is sent as one single block that must follow one fixed route
It is split into packets that may take different routes; the client reassembles them once all are received
It is split into packets, and the server reassembles them before sending
It cannot be sent over HTTP: large files require FTP

explanation: Big responses are cut into packets sent separately, possibly along different routes of the network. The client (the receiver) rebuilds the full response once it has received all the packets.

distractor_notes.a: Packets are routed independently; there is no single block on one fixed route.
distractor_notes.c: Reassembly is done by the receiver (the client), not by the sender.
distractor_notes.d: HTTP transports large files and images every day; FTP is just another protocol.

stem: You type `https://github.com/tensorflow` in your browser. In which order do the following steps happen?

options.text: HTTP request -> DNS resolution -> TCP connection to port 443 -> rendering of the HTML -> HTTP response
TCP connection to port 443 -> DNS resolution -> HTTP request -> HTTP response -> rendering of the HTML
DNS resolution -> TCP connection to port 443 -> HTTP request -> HTTP response -> rendering of the HTML
DNS resolution -> HTTP request -> TCP connection to port 80 -> HTTP response -> rendering of the HTML

explanation: The browser first needs the server's IP address (DNS resolution), then opens a TCP connection to that IP on port 443 (the default for https), sends the HTTP request over it, receives the HTTP response (in packets) and finally renders the HTML.

distractor_notes.a: The request can only be sent over an established connection, and rendering needs the response.
distractor_notes.b: You cannot connect before knowing the IP address: DNS resolution comes first.
distractor_notes.d: The connection must exist before the request is sent, and https uses port 443, not 80.

verify.reference: Slides 289-297 'Life of an HTTP request' (DNS resolution, port, TCP connection, request, response, rendering)

stem: Which IP address always refers to **your own computer** (the hostname `localhost`)?
explanation: 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address: a request sent to it never leaves your machine, and `localhost` is its hostname. This is where a Flask app started on your computer can be reached.

distractor_notes.b: A typical private address on a home network (often the router), not your own machine in general.
distractor_notes.c: 0.0.0.0 means 'unspecified / all interfaces' (a server can listen on it); it is not the loopback address.

stem: Once the browser knows the IP address of `github.com`, what is established between the client and the server **before** the HTTP request is sent?

options.text: A new DNS entry on the server
A TCP connection to the server's port (443 for https)
A copy of the HTML page stored at the ISP
Nothing: the HTTP request is the first thing exchanged

explanation: The client opens a TCP connection to IP:port of the server (e.g. 140.82.118.4:443); the HTTP request and the HTTP response then travel over this connection.

distractor_notes.a: DNS resolution already happened on the client side; the server's DNS table is not modified.
distractor_notes.c: The ISP relays the traffic but does not pre-store the page.
distractor_notes.d: HTTP is sent over an already established TCP connection.

stem: Which of the following is correct about servers?

options.text: The word 'server' can refer both to the program answering requests and to the computer running it.
One computer can run several servers (HTTP, API, mail, database...), each listening on its own port.
An HTTPS server listens on port 443 by default.
All of the above.

explanation: All three statements are true: 'server' designates both the program and the machine; a machine can host several server programs, distinguished by their ports; and HTTPS servers listen on port 443 unless configured otherwise.

distractor_notes.a: True, but not the only true statement.
distractor_notes.b: True, but not the only true statement.
distractor_notes.c: True, but not the only true statement.

verify.reference: Slide 284 (servers = programs and computers), slide 292 (several servers, ports, HTTPS 443), slide 316

stem: Which statement about DNS is **false**?

options.text: It maps domain names such as `github.com` to IP addresses.
If a DNS server does not know a domain name, it can ask other servers recursively.
DNS servers listen on port 53 by default.
DNS resolution is performed by the web server after it has received the HTTP request.

explanation: DNS resolution happens on the client side (browser + the ISP's DNS servers) **before** connecting: the client needs the IP address to reach the web server at all. Statements a, b and c are true.

distractor_notes.a: True: this is the purpose of DNS.
distractor_notes.b: True: unknown names are resolved by recursively asking other nodes.
distractor_notes.c: True: 53 is the default DNS port.

verify.reference: Slide 291 'DNS resolution'; slide 300 (the browser does DNS resolution); slide 316 (53 for DNS)

stem: The machine `140.82.118.4` runs an HTTPS server on port 443, a MySQL server on port 3306 and a Redis server on port 6379. A client opens `http://140.82.118.4/status`. Which program receives the request?

options.text: The HTTPS server, because it is the only web server on the machine
The MySQL server
The Redis server
None of them: `http://` without an explicit port means port 80, where no server listens

explanation: When the URL has no port, the client uses the default port of the scheme: 80 for http (443 only for https). Nothing listens on port 80 on this machine, so the connection is refused; the HTTPS server is never contacted.

distractor_notes.a: 443 is the default for https, not for http: the scheme decides the default port.
distractor_notes.b: 3306 would only be used if written explicitly in the URL.
distractor_notes.c: 6379 would only be used if written explicitly in the URL.

verify.reference: Slide 300 (the browser adds the port based on the protocol); slide 316 (80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS)

stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse

u = urlparse('https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow')
print(u.netloc)

options.text: github.com
https://github.com
tensorflow
/tensorflow/tensorflow

explanation: `netloc` (network location) is the host part, between `//` and the path. The scheme is in `u.scheme` ('https') and the path in `u.path` ('/tensorflow/tensorflow').

distractor_notes.b: The scheme is not part of netloc.
distractor_notes.c: tensorflow is part of the path (the requested resource).

stem: What will be the output of the code?
code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse

u = urlparse('https://www.google.com/search?q=ip+address')
print(u.port)

options.text: None

explanation: `.port` only returns a port written explicitly in the URL. None is written here, so it is None - even though the browser will connect to port 443, the default for https.

distractor_notes.a: 443 is the port the browser will use, but urlparse does not fill in default ports.
distractor_notes.c: 80 is the default for http, and it is not filled in either.
distractor_notes.d: A missing port is None, not 0.

stem: What is the output of the following code?

options.text: {'q': ['ip+address'], 'lang': ['en']}
{'q': 'ip address', 'lang': 'en'}
{'q': ['ip address'], 'lang': ['en']}
{'q=ip+address': ['lang=en']}

explanation: Query parameters are separated by `&`, and each `name=value` pair is decoded (`+` becomes a space). parse_qs returns a dict whose values are **lists**, because the same name may appear several times in a query.

distractor_notes.a: Decoding turns `+` back into a space.
distractor_notes.b: parse_qs always gives lists of values.
distractor_notes.d: `&` separates parameters and `=` separates a name from its value.

stem: Spaces are not allowed in a URL query. What is the output of the following code?
code:
from urllib.parse import quote_plus

print(quote_plus('ip address'))

options.text: ip+address
ip%20address
ip_address
ip address

explanation: `quote_plus` escapes a value for a query string: spaces become `+`, as in `https://www.google.com/search?q=ip+address`.

distractor_notes.b: That is what `quote` (without _plus) produces: %20 is the percent-encoding of a space.
distractor_notes.c: Underscores are never used to escape spaces.
distractor_notes.d: A space cannot appear in a URL; it must be escaped.

stem: Find the output of the code?
code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse

u = urlparse('https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln#The_Civil_War')
print(u.path, u.fragment)

options.text: /wiki/Abraham_Lincoln The_Civil_War
/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln #The_Civil_War
wiki/Abraham_Lincoln The_Civil_War
/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln#The_Civil_War The_Civil_War

explanation: The fragment is everything after `#`, without the `#` itself, and it is not part of the path. The path keeps its leading `/`.

distractor_notes.b: The `#` separator is not included in `fragment`.

stem: True or False: when the browser opens `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python#History`, the fragment `#History` is sent to the server in the HTTP request.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The fragment is never sent to the server: the request only asks for `/wiki/Python`. The browser uses the fragment itself, once the page is received, to move the focus to the part of the document named `History`.

distractor_notes.a: The request URL stops before `#`: the fragment is handled by the client only.

verify.reference: Slide 319 'Fragments': the fragment is not passed to the server

stem: Which of the following gives the parts of a URL in the correct order?

options.text: host://scheme:port/path?fragment#query
scheme://host:port@username:password/path#fragment?query
scheme://username:password@host:port/path?query#fragment
scheme://host/path:port?query#fragment

explanation: General form: the scheme (protocol), optional user info followed by `@`, the host, an optional `:port`, the path, an optional `?query`, and an optional `#fragment` at the very end.

distractor_notes.a: The scheme comes first, and the query (?) precedes the fragment (#).
distractor_notes.b: User info comes before the host, and the fragment is always last.
distractor_notes.d: The port belongs to the host part, before the path.

stem: What is the default port of an HTTPS server, used when a URL starting with `https://` does not specify one?
explanation: Some ports are implicit: 80 for HTTP and 443 for HTTPS. The browser adds the port matching the scheme when it is not written in the URL.

distractor_notes.a: 80 is the default for plain HTTP.
distractor_notes.d: 8000 is the port used by `python -m http.server`, not a standard HTTPS port.

verify.reference: Slide 316 '80 for HTTP server by default (443 HTTPS)'; slide 292 'HTTPS servers listen to 443'
